headline: A judge approves Bayer's deal on Roundup cancer claims

sources.title: Bayer agrees to pay Roundup claims in settlement that could cost billions (NPR)
Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer settlement for Roundup cancer claims (BBC)
Court approves $7.25 billion settlement with Bayer over claims Roundup weed killer caused cancer (AP)

chunks.text: On November 20, 2026, a judge in Missouri {{signed off on}} a [[settlement]] over the [[weed killer]] Roundup, which kills unwanted plants. A settlement is a deal that ends a court case. Bayer, Roundup's German owner, will {{set aside}} up to 7.25 billion dollars in a [[special fund]]. The money is for Roundup users who have a kind of blood cancer or get it later. Many [[sued]], or asked courts to make the company pay.

verbs.wrong: To sell a business to a rival

verbs.correct: To keep money for a special use
verbs.wrong: To win money in a court case
verbs.why: She sets aside a little money every month for her kids. Many families set aside cash for a new car. Bayer will set aside up to 7.25 billion dollars in a special fund.

chunks.text: Patients link their illness to the main [[ingredient]] in Roundup, a chemical. Bayer [[denies]] this. The argument {{goes back}} more than ten years. In 2015, a World Health Organization cancer agency said the chemical probably causes cancer. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has said it is not likely to cause cancer when used [[as directed]]. Bayer {{took the chemical out}} of new Roundup for home gardens, but farms still use it.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a past time
verbs.why: This bakery goes back to the 1950s. Their friendship goes back to high school. The argument over the main chemical in Roundup goes back more than ten years.

verbs.correct: To remove something from a product
verbs.wrong: To sell something at a lower price
verbs.why: The company takes the sugar out of its new drinks. Some bakers take the salt out of their bread. Bayer took the chemical out of new Roundup for home gardens.

chunks.text: The deal {{spells out}} how much [[compensation]], or money for [[harm]], each person can get. Average payments range from 10,000 to 165,000 dollars. [[Farm workers]] who got sick before 60 could get the most. Some patients' lawyers {{pushed back}}, saying the payments were too small. Others said that without the deal, patients could {{end up}} with nothing. The judge did not want to {{hold up}} payments to sick people.

verbs.why: The contract spells out the hours for each worker. My teacher spells out the class rules on the first day. The deal spells out how much each person can get.
Workers often push back when a company cuts their pay. Parents push back against the new school hours. Some patients' lawyers pushed back, saying the payments were too small.

verbs.wrong: To speak to a judge in court
verbs.why: People who never save money often end up with big debts. Many people who skip breakfast end up very hungry by noon. Other lawyers said that without the deal, patients could end up with nothing.
Bad weather often holds up flights. One missing form holds up the whole process. The judge did not want to hold up payments to sick people.

chunks.text: The judge said if he had {{turned down}} the deal, Bayer might have asked for [[bankruptcy]] protection. That is a court process for companies that cannot pay their [[debts]]. Bayer has {{gone through}} years of [[costly]] [[court fights]] over about 200,000 [[claims]], or requests for money. Its [[legal bills]] have {{piled up}}. In June 2026, the highest U.S. court ruled that people cannot sue Bayer in state courts for not warning about cancer. Bayer hopes the deal will {{wrap up}} most of the [[remaining cases]].

mainIdea.s: A U.S. judge approved a deal in which Bayer will pay up to 7.25 billion dollars to Roundup users with a blood cancer. The company still denies that its weed killer causes the illness.
mainIdea.why: A judge in Missouri signed off on the settlement on November 20, 2026. Bayer denies that Roundup causes cancer, and the science is still in dispute.

mainIdea.s: A court in Missouri decided that Roundup causes a kind of blood cancer and ordered Bayer to pay. Because of that finding, farms across America must stop using the weed killer.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the court did not decide that Roundup causes cancer. It approved a deal, Bayer denies the cancer link, and farms still use the chemical.

mainIdea.s: Farmers in several U.S. states are switching to a cheaper weed killer this season because prices rose. Sellers say the new product works well on corn, wheat and soybean fields.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a court deal. Bayer will set aside up to 7.25 billion dollars for Roundup users with a kind of blood cancer.

tf.s: A judge in Missouri signed off on Bayer's Roundup settlement.
tf.why: The judge gave final approval to the settlement on November 20, 2026.

tf.s: Bayer now agrees that Roundup causes cancer.
tf.why: Bayer denies that Roundup causes cancer, even though the argument over the chemical goes back more than ten years.

tf.s: Health experts all agree that the chemical in Roundup is safe.
tf.why: A cancer agency of the World Health Organization said it probably causes cancer, but the U.S. agency has said it is not likely to. The argument over the chemical goes back more than ten years.

tf.s: Some lawyers pushed back because they think the payments are too small.
tf.why: Some lawyers for patients said the payments are too small, while others said that without the deal patients could end up with nothing.

tf.s: The judge wanted to hold up payments to sick people.
tf.why: The judge did not want to hold up payments. He also said Bayer might have asked for bankruptcy protection if he had turned down the deal.

tf.s: Bayer hopes the deal will wrap up most of the remaining Roundup cases.
tf.why: Bayer has gone through years of costly court fights and hopes this deal will end most of them.

lines.text: Did you hear that a judge {{signed off on}} the big Roundup deal?
The weed killer? What's the deal about?
Thousands of Roundup users with a kind of blood cancer sued Bayer. They say Roundup made them sick.
No. Bayer denies it, and the science is still in dispute. [[Who's to say]] who is right?
So how much money are we talking about?
Up to 7.25 billion dollars. Bayer will {{set aside}} money in a fund every year for up to 21 years.
Does everyone get the same amount?
No. The deal {{spells out}} average payments from about 10,000 to 165,000 dollars.
I bet the money was [[a touchy subject]].
It was. Some lawyers {{pushed back}} and said the payments are too small.
Every deal like this has its [[pros and cons]].
Right. Other lawyers said that without the deal, patients could {{end up}} with nothing, and the judge didn't want to {{hold up}} the money.
So is Bayer [[in the clear]] now?
Not totally. The company hopes the deal will {{wrap up}} most of the remaining cases, not all of them.
After all those court fights, I'm sure Bayer wants to [[turn the page]].
For sure. It has {{gone through}} years of them, and its legal bills have {{piled up}}.
